# Biḷāravatajātaka (Ja 128)

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Biḷāravatajātaka* (Ja 128), also referred to as the *Bilārajātaka*, is an animal tale preserved in the Pali *Jātaka* collection [Appleton 2010]. The story of the present is set at Jetavana, where the Buddha delivers the discourse regarding a hypocritical monk, remarking that the monk had similarly practiced hypocrisy in past lives.

In the story of the past, a predator (depicted as a cat in verse and as a jackal in the prose narrative) poses as a pious ascetic to gain the trust of a community of mice or rats, surreptitiously catching and devouring the last of the company as they depart each day [Appleton; Appleton 2010]. The Bodhisatta, appearing as the wise leader of the rodent group, detects the deception, catches the creature as it prepares to pounce, and bites its throat to kill it, after which the rest of the company devours the carcass [Appleton; Appleton 2010]. Modern scholars highlight the story as an animal fable where the Bodhisatta violates the primary precept against taking life to defeat an adversary, illustrating the tension between folk narrative motifs and orthodox Buddhist ideals [Appleton; Appleton 2010].

The central verse cited in scholarly analysis (*yo ve dhammaṃ dhajaṃ katvā, nigūḷho pāpam ācare...*) warns against hoisting the banner of Dhamma while secretly practicing wickedness, designating such deceit as the "practice of a cat" (*biḷāra-vata*), which the commentary (Jā I 461) explains as hypocritical conduct (*kerātika-vata*) [Marino 2017].
